lines: A team I know calls their dashboard real time. It's an hourly cron job.
Nobody had ever actually put a number on how long one order sits before it shows up.
So I took the exact same stream of orders and ran it through three different ingestion modes, and watched one single row's own delay in each.
Before the numbers, the vocabulary every one of these modes shares, because you'll need it for the rest of this chapter.
Every pipeline has a source, where the truth lives, a sink, where it lands, and a cursor, the record of how far it's gotten.

And a buffer, where bytes wait their turn. In a pull, the consumer decides when to ask, so the source ends up holding that buffer. Flip to a push, and the source decides when to send, so the consumer has to hold it instead.
Here's a question before I show you the measurements.
Batch moves the most rows in a single run, that's not in dispute.
So which mode actually drops the most unplanned load on whatever has to consume it: batch, because of the size of its runs, or streaming?
answer: The trap is that batch really does move the most rows at once, so it's tempting to call that the heaviest load.
But batch does that work on a schedule the consumer itself agreed to. It's never a surprise.
Streaming hands the consumer whatever the producer sends, whenever it sends it. No schedule, no shield. That's where an unplanned surge actually comes from.

lines: I generated one fixed stream of three hundred simulated orders and read it three ways: once an hour, once every thirty seconds, and continuously.
The average wait for a single order dropped from thousands of seconds, down to tens of seconds, down to under one second, in that order.
And the size of each delivery dropped the same way: roughly a hundred rows handed over at once under the hourly read, down to well under one row at a time under the continuous read.
Same shrinking interval, counted a different way: how many moving parts each mode actually needs.
The hourly read needs exactly one: the scheduled job itself. Nothing watches whether it actually ran.
Add a checkpoint of your last position and you've got the thirty second read, and a new failure: lots of small, separately recorded runs piling up behind you.
Go fully continuous and you need a broker, a consumer, and that consumer's own tracked position, three parts, and the backlog failure we already named has nowhere left to hide.
So: four positions in every pipeline, and pull and push decide which side holds the buffer.
Three ways to cut the identical stream, measured, not guessed: thousands of seconds down to under one, a hundred rows at once down to well under one.
And one honest failure mode for each: a late run nobody notices, small runs piling up, or a backlog with nothing to shield it. Pick your mode by which of those three you can actually live with.
